program_note:
Of Love and Loss presents the broad outlines of a story.  In the first movement, “Love Dance,” two people meet, start dancing together, and fall in love.  In the second movement, “Lullaby,” the couple sing a tender and slow—yet energetic—lullaby to their new-born baby.  In the last movement, “Lament,” there has been a catastrophe, and each believes the other to have died.  At the end they are reunited, although perhaps only in the memory of the love and tenderness they shared.

It also tells a more traditional musical story, with a sonata-form movement, a middle-movement romanze, and a rondo-form movement—all typical of a late 18th- or early 19th-century concerto, but with just one exception:  the sonata- and rondo- form movements are switched in their order of appearance.  Thus the rondo appears first, preceded by a slow introduction, and the sonata appears last.

The slow introduction to the first movement—Love Dance (Introduction and Rondo)—is characterized by a pair of gently oscillating chords, above which float the slightly-melancholy solo lines.  This is followed by the main melodic idea of the rondo, the first of a series of Spanish-influenced dance tunes accompanied by jaunty rhythms in the ensemble.  The rondo proceeds much as that in Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto does, except that the alternating sections become shorter and shorter.  This formal acceleration is interrupted by a brief cadenza by the two soloists, but is then resumed as the movement draws to a close.

The second movement, the Lullaby, is subtitled Berceuse, a typical 19th-century character piece usually featuring a rocking motion in triplets intended to lull a baby to sleep.  Here, the triplet idea can be found in the solo lines, as well as in the three-beat groupings of the melody over the four-beat groupings of the accompaniment.  But this juxtaposition is usually quite subtle, especially since the accompaniment grows out of the clarinet solo line itself.

The last movement, Lament, is subtitled Threnody, an ancient Greek form expressing a strong feeling of grief for the dead.  In ancient Greece, these lamentations would traditionally have been performed on the aulos, a double-reed instrument and a predecessor to the modern oboe.  In this movement, the ensemble takes a very active role expressing the horror and fear of the catastrophe, most especially in their exposition.  Contrasting with the narrowly-twisting ensemble lines, the soloists melodic lines in their own (second) exposition feature huge jumps from one register to another.  The rage of both themes is then followed by the beginning of grief-filled acceptance in a contrasting slower section.  But the real grief is saved for the long cadenza, in which long, mournful melodies in both the oboe and clarinet are made even more poignant by the way that they rub against each other.  As the soloists gradually come to recall their earlier love, the ensemble interrupts with one last outpouring of anger, which exhausts itself and transforms into one final recollection.

The total duration is approximately 25:30, with the individual movements approximately 7:50, 6:30, and 11:00.

Of Love and Loss is dedicated to Marion Kuszyk, Gary Gray, Thomas Lee and the UCLA Wind Ensemble, who premiered it on 26 May, 2004.

David S. Lefkowitz

Los Angeles, California

19 August, 2004
